title: Debt III: Treasuries, agencies, CMOs, and the money market

reading.body:
Marketable Treasuries carry the **full faith and credit** of the U.S. government and are the credit-risk-free benchmark. All are **book-entry**, sold at auction (noncompetitive bids up to **$10 million** get the auction-set yield), and **non-callable** (none issued callable since 1985). Minimum is **$100** and increments of $100. Interest is **taxable federally, exempt from state and local tax**; capital gains are taxable everywhere.

By maturity: **T-bills** (one year or less — 4/8/13/26/52-week benchmarks, sold at a discount, no coupon), **T-notes** (2, 3, 5, 7, 10 years; semiannual coupons; quoted in 32nds), **T-bonds** (20 and 30 years). Bills are the 'risk-free rate' in most exam questions.

**TIPS** carry a fixed coupon rate applied to a principal that is **adjusted for inflation (CPI)**, so the dollar interest rises with prices. On a $1,000 TIPS with a 3% coupon, if inflation runs 4% the principal grows to about $1,040 and the coupon is paid on that: 3% × $1,040 = **$31.20** for the year. The **inflation adjustment to principal is taxed as ordinary income in the year it accrues** even though no cash is received — 'phantom income,' so TIPS belong in tax-deferred accounts. At maturity you get the greater of the adjusted or original principal (a deflation floor).

**STRIPS** are Treasuries stripped into zero-coupon pieces with **direct** government backing — bought at a discount, maturing at par, maximum interest-rate risk, no reinvestment risk, and annual accretion taxed as interest (phantom income again).

reading.h: Agencies: GNMA vs GSEs vs the state-exempt lenders
reading.body:
**Ginnie Mae (GNMA)** — a government corporation in HUD — guarantees **pass-through certificates** backed by FHA/VA-insured mortgages, paying **monthly** interest *and* principal. It is the **only** mortgage-backed security with **full faith and credit**. **Fannie Mae** and **Freddie Mac** are **GSEs** — publicly traded, chartered by Congress, with **implicit** backing only (both in federal conservatorship since 2008).

Taxation is the trap: GNMA, FNMA, and FHLMC interest is **fully taxable — federal, state, and local**. The **exceptions** are three lender agencies — **FHLB, FFCB (Farm Credit), and TVA** — whose interest is **state- and local-tax-exempt** (taxable federally), the reverse of the mortgage agencies. Sallie Mae (SLM) was privatized in 2004 and carries no government backing.

Homeowners can prepay their mortgages any time — and that reshapes a mortgage security's cash flow. When rates **fall**, homeowners refinance, principal comes back **early**, and it must be reinvested at the new lower rates — **prepayment risk** (and MBS price gains are capped near par, 'negative convexity'). When rates **rise**, refinancing stops, so the principal comes back **later** and the average life **stretches** — **extension risk**.

Because of this uncertainty, mortgage securities are measured by **average life**, not a fixed maturity, and they yield **more** than Treasuries. The **PSA** model expresses prepayment speed: 100% PSA is the benchmark assumption, 200% PSA is twice as fast.

A **collateralized mortgage obligation (CMO)** pours a pool of pass-throughs into **tranches** with different maturities and priorities, so investors can choose a more predictable average life. CMOs pay **monthly**, come in **$1,000** denominations, and are **fully taxable** at all levels.

- **Sequential-pay** — tranches retire in order (A first, then B…).
- **PAC (Planned Amortization Class)** — protected against **both** prepayment and extension risk by companion tranches; **most stable, lowest yield** — the safest for conservative retail.
- **TAC** — protected against prepayment risk **only**; yields more than a PAC.
- **Companion/support** — absorbs the variability; **highest risk and yield, least suitable**.
- **Z-tranche** — receives no cash until earlier tranches retire (interest accrues like a zero); longest, most volatile, phantom income.
- **PO (principal-only)** — benefits from *faster* prepayments (rates down → price up).
- **IO (interest-only)** — value **rises when rates rise** (slower prepayments keep interest flowing) — the one bond-like security whose price moves *with* rates.

reading.h: Rule 2216 — how CMOs may be communicated
reading.body:
Because retail investors mistake CMOs for CDs, **FINRA Rule 2216** governs their retail communications. Key requirements: the product name must include '**Collateralized Mortgage Obligation**'; the communication may **not compare a CMO to any other investment, especially a bank CD**; it must disclose that any government-agency backing applies **only to the face value, not to any premium paid**, and that **yield and average life will fluctuate** with prepayments and rates. Before selling to a **non-institutional** customer, the firm must **offer educational material**. Any yield shown must be accompanied by the coupon, price, **PSA prepayment assumption**, and estimated **average life**.

The throughline: a CMO is *not* a guaranteed, fixed-maturity, CD-like product, and the communication rules exist to stop that impression.

reading.h: Money market, the rate ladder, and international debt
reading.body:
Money market instruments mature in **one year or less** and are mostly sold at a discount: **T-bills** (safest), **commercial paper** (unsecured corporate, ≤ 270 days), **banker's acceptances** (import/export, ≤ 270 days), **negotiable CDs** (≥ $100,000, pay interest at par), **repos**, **fed funds**, and **Eurodollar deposits**. The **rate ladder**, low to high: **fed funds < discount rate < broker call rate < prime rate** (the Fed funds rate, set by supply/demand between banks, is the most volatile).

International debt: a **Eurodollar bond** is a U.S.-dollar bond issued **outside** the U.S. — **not SEC-registered**. A **Yankee bond** is a dollar bond issued **in** the U.S. by a **foreign** issuer — SEC-registered, prospectus required. **ETNs** are unsecured bank debt — the holder bears the **issuer's credit risk** (a trap: they are not funds).

flashcards.back: $100 minimum; non-callable (since 1985); interest federal-taxable, state/local-exempt. Noncompetitive bid ≤ $10M.
Fixed coupon rate on a CPI-adjusted principal. $1,000 TIPS, 3%, 4% inflation → principal $1,040, interest $31.20; principal growth taxed annually (phantom income).
Treasuries stripped into zeros with direct government backing; bought at discount, mature at par; max rate risk; phantom income.
Only MBS with full faith and credit; monthly interest AND principal; interest FULLY taxable (federal, state, local).
GSEs — publicly traded, implicit backing only; in conservatorship since 2008; fully taxable.
FHLB, FFCB (Farm Credit), TVA — interest exempt from state/local tax (reverse of the mortgage agencies).
Rates fall → refinance → principal early (prepayment). Rates rise → refinancing stops → average life stretches (extension).
PAC = most prepayment+extension protection, lowest yield, safest. Companion/support = highest risk & yield.
IO rises in value when rates RISE (slower prepayments). PO benefits from faster prepayments (rates down → price up).
CMO retail communications may NOT compare a CMO to another investment, especially a bank CD; must offer educational material and disclose PSA/average life.
Fed funds < discount rate < broker call rate < prime rate.
Eurodollar = USD bond issued OUTSIDE the U.S., NOT SEC-registered. Yankee = USD bond issued IN the U.S. by a foreign issuer, SEC-registered.

quiz.stem: An investor buys a $1,000 TIPS with a 3% coupon. Over the first year the CPI rises 4%. Approximately how much interest will the investor receive for the year?
quiz.explanation: TIPS keep the coupon rate fixed and adjust the principal for inflation: $1,000 × 1.04 = $1,040, and 3% of $1,040 = $31.20. The inflation adjustment raises principal (taxed annually as phantom income), not the coupon rate — so $30.00 (no adjustment) and $70.00 (adding 4% to 3%) are traps.

quiz.stem: Which of the following CMO tranches would be expected to INCREASE in value when market interest rates rise?
quiz.explanation: Rising rates slow prepayments, so the mortgage interest stream lasts longer and the IO tranche gains value — the one bond-like security whose price moves with rates. POs benefit from faster prepayments, and PAC and Z tranches lose value like ordinary bonds.

quiz.stem: All of the following statements about Ginnie Mae (GNMA) pass-through certificates are true EXCEPT:
options: They are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government
Investors receive monthly payments of both interest and principal
The underlying pools consist of FHA- or VA-insured mortgages
Interest received is exempt from state and local income taxes
quiz.explanation: GNMA interest is fully taxable at the federal, state, and local levels — only Treasuries and the FHLB/FFCB/TVA lenders get the state exemption. The other three statements are the classic true attributes of GNMA pass-throughs.

quiz.stem: When short-term Treasury yields are higher than long-term Treasury yields, the yield curve is described as:
quiz.explanation: An inverted (negative) curve has short rates above long rates, typically during Fed tightening when markets expect cuts. A normal curve slopes upward, a flat curve shows little difference, and a humped curve peaks at intermediate maturities.

quiz.stem: A conservative retiree wants monthly income from a CMO but is worried about both early and late return of principal. Which tranche is MOST suitable?
quiz.explanation: A PAC is protected against both prepayment and extension risk by its companion tranches, giving the most predictable average life — the safest CMO for a conservative investor. The companion, Z, and IO tranches all carry high or unusual risk and are least suitable.

quiz.stem: Interest on which of the following is exempt from state and local income tax?
quiz.explanation: FFCB, like FHLB and TVA, is a lender agency whose interest is exempt from state and local tax (taxable federally). GNMA, FNMA, and CMOs are all fully taxable at every level — the reverse-attribute trap.

quiz.stem: Which of the following short-term rates is normally the LOWEST?
quiz.explanation: The rate ladder from low to high is fed funds < discount rate < broker call rate < prime rate, so the fed funds rate (overnight bank-to-bank lending) is normally the lowest. Prime, the banks' best-customer rate, is the highest.

quiz.stem: A U.S.-dollar-denominated bond issued OUTSIDE the United States and not registered with the SEC is BEST described as a:
quiz.explanation: A Eurodollar bond is a U.S.-dollar bond issued outside the U.S. and is not SEC-registered. A Yankee bond is the opposite — a dollar bond issued in the U.S. by a foreign issuer, which is SEC-registered.
